content: Bronchiectasis is increasingly being recognized as a significant contributor to chronic lung disease in both adults and children across highand low-income countries. This condition is characterized by irreversible airway dilatation, often accompanied by persistent airway inflammation and chronic bacterial infections. The primary goal of medical management is to alleviate symptoms, reduce the frequency of exacerbations, improve quality of life, and prevent disease progression. This review is an update of a previous analysis first published in 2000. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in children and adults with stable bronchiectasis. Specifically, the review aimed to determine whether ICS use reduces the severity and frequency of acute respiratory exacerbations or impacts the long-term decline in pulmonary function. The literature search included databases such as the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials, MEDLINE, and Embase, with the most recent search conducted in June 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ICS with either a placebo or no treatment. Participants included children and adults with clinical or radiographic evidence of bronchiectasis, excluding individuals with cystic fibrosis. Seven studies involving 380 adult participants were included in the review, with 348 completing the studies. Due to variability in reported outcomes across the studies, only limited meta-analyses could be performed for both short-term ICS use (6 months or less) and long-term ICS use (greater than 6 months). For short-term ICS use, data from two studies showed no significant differences in lung function parameters, such as forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1) (mean difference [MD] -0.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.26 to 0.09) and forced vital capacity (FVC) (MD 0.01 L, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.17), when compared to no ICS use. Similarly, there were no significant differences in the frequency of exacerbations (MD 0.09, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.79) or health-related quality of life (HRQoL) scores. However, data were limited. One non-placebo-controlled study reported a marginal but statistically significant improvement in sputum volume and dyspnea scores with ICS use, though clinical data could not be extracted. For long-term ICS use (over 6 months), a single study examined lung function and other clinical outcomes but found no significant effects of ICS on any measured outcomes. Adverse effects could not be adequately assessed due to limited data availability. Although all seven studies claimed to be double-blind, one short-term ICS study was judged to have a high risk of bias due to issues with blinding, attrition, and outcome reporting. The overall quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE framework, was low for all outcomes. This was attributed to factors such as the inclusion of non-placebo-controlled trials, indirectness, imprecision, and the small number of participants and studies. In conclusion, this updated review found insufficient evidence to support the routine use of ICS in adults with stable bronchiectasis. Additionally, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the use of ICS during acute exacerbations in adults or in children with bronchiectasis, as no studies addressed these scenarios.
